tools.name: mcp__dc2c4692-a6c6-4edb-8301-12e868909281__firecrawl_scrape
tools.description: Scrape one URL and return its content, or execute catalogued Alexandria capabilities. URL mode returns markdown by default, or HTML, links, screenshots, branding data, a targeted answer, or JSON matching a supplied schema, plus page metadata. Firecrawl may serve recently indexed content; set `maxAge: 0` for a live fetch. A successful response does not by itself confirm the page is still current. Browser actions can change the live page when interactive actions are enabled, and a named browser profile can load saved session data and overwrite its stored state. `firecrawl_search` with `sources` unset and `firecrawl_find_tools` can discover providers for the same fields across several pages; a matching Alexandria provider returns typed records in one call. Alexandria mode: `alexandria` selects catalogued capability execution and is mutually exclusive with `url`. Alexandria execution is billed at the capability's listed price and needs a team with Alexandria enabled.

requestId.description: Idempotency key bound to one Alexandria execution payload. Generated when omitted and returned with the result.

alexandria.description: Catalogued Alexandria capability invocation, mutually exclusive with url. One {provider, capability, options} object or an array of 1-10, with contracts available through firecrawl_search or firecrawl_find_tools. Each call may include version to pin a published workflow; omitting it uses latest. Only requestId and timeout are supported alongside alexandria. The selected contract marks required inputs and any requiresOneOf groups (at least one member per group); it may include example.request/example.response and response.key (which may differ from records). Where pagination is declared, its fields govern paging with the same filters; catalogue next is separate from provider pagination. Returns per-capability results in data.alexandria with data, records, or an error with a code; individual capabilities can fail even when the outer response succeeds. Requires an API key on a team with Alexandria enabled. Some providers require accepted terms; blocked requests return the applicable requirements.

capability.description: Capability address as returned by search or discover, e.g. "series/observations".

version.description: Optional published workflow version. Omit to use the latest version.

options.description: Capability options as declared by its contract.

tools.name: mcp__dc2c4692-a6c6-4edb-8301-12e868909281__firecrawl_search
tools.description: Search web and specialized indexes, returning ranked results with query-relevant highlights. Each web result is a title, URL, and description. Operators include quoted phrases, `-term`, `site:host`, `inurl:term`, `intitle:term`, and `related:host`; the set is non-exhaustive. `includeDomains` and `excludeDomains` are mutually exclusive hostname filters; categories limit result types to `research`, `pdf`, or `developer`. For a programming question, add `categories: ["developer"]`. It searches an index of public repositories, GitHub issues, merged pull requests, repository READMEs, and code documentation, and returns the results in `data.web` with `category: "developer"`. Authenticated search combines web results, semantic tool summaries and domain matches. Use sources: ["alexandria"] for semantic tools only. A search with sources: ["web"] omits semantic provider discovery; domainTools: true can still return website-matched tools. Web-only results use domainTools: false. Tool matches describe available structured-data capabilities, not executed data. toolDetail: "compact" (default) returns only provider, capability and description; "summary" adds metadata; "full" includes their input and output contracts. firecrawl_scrape with an alexandria body executes a selected capability; firecrawl_find_tools provides catalogue browsing and full contracts. Returns result groups in `data` and an operation `id`.

Operators include quoted phrases, `-term`, `site:host`, `inurl:term`, `intitle:term`, and `related:host`; the set is non-exhaustive. `includeDomains` and `excludeDomains` are mutually exclusive hostname filters; categories limit result types to `research`, `pdf`, or `developer`. For a programming question, add `categories: ["developer"]`. It searches an index of public repositories, GitHub issues, merged pull requests, repository READMEs, and code documentation, and returns the results in `data.web` with `category: "developer"`. Authenticated search combines web results, semantic tool summaries and domain matches. Use sources: ["alexandria"] for semantic tools only. A search with sources: ["web"] omits semantic provider discovery; domainTools: true can still return website-matched tools. Web-only results use domainTools: false. Tool matches describe available structured-data capabilities, not executed data. toolDetail: "compact" (default) returns only provider, capability and description; "summary" adds metadata; "full" includes their input and output contracts. firecrawl_scrape with an alexandria body executes a selected capability; firecrawl_find_tools provides catalogue browsing and full contracts. Returns result groups in `data` and an operation `id`.

toolDetail.description: Compact by default. Compact returns only provider, capability and description; full includes contracts. Inspect selected compact tools with firecrawl_find_tools providers and capabilities.

query.description: Query for web and semantic tool discovery. Operators include quoted phrases, `-term`, `site:host`, `inurl:term`, `intitle:term`, and `related:host`; the set is non-exhaustive. Catalogue browsing is available through firecrawl_find_tools.

domainTools.description: Include domain-matched tools for result URLs. Defaults to true when Alexandria is combined with web, news or images; semantic-only search leaves domain matching off.

## claude-in-chrome
**IMPORTANT: If the Chrome browser tools are deferred (must be loaded via ToolSearch before use), load them with ToolSearch before calling them, and batch every tool you expect to need into ONE ToolSearch call (the select query accepts a comma-separated list). Do NOT load tools one at a time; each separate ToolSearch call wastes a full round-trip.**

Start a browser task whose tools are not yet loaded with a single call loading the core set:

ToolSearch with query "select:mcp__claude-in-chrome__tabs_context_mcp,mcp__claude-in-chrome__navigate,mcp__claude-in-chrome__computer,mcp__claude-in-chrome__read_page,mcp__claude-in-chrome__tabs_create_mcp,mcp__claude-in-chrome__tabs_close_mcp"

Add task-specific tools to the same call when the task obviously needs them: read_console_messages / read_network_requests for debugging, form_input for forms, gif_creator for recordings, javascript_tool for page scripting. Only issue a second ToolSearch if the task later needs a tool you did not anticipate.

## computer-use
You have a computer-use MCP available (tools named `mcp__computer-use__*`). It lets you take screenshots of the user's desktop and control it with mouse clicks, keyboard input, and scrolling.

**Pick the right tool for the app.** Each tier trades speed/precision against coverage:

1. **Dedicated MCP for the app** — if the task is in an app that has its own MCP (Slack, Gmail, Calendar, Linear, etc.) and that MCP is connected, use it. API-backed tools are fast and precise.
2. **Chrome MCP** (`mcp__claude-in-chrome__*`) — if the target is a web app and there's no dedicated MCP for it, use the browser tools. DOM-aware, much faster than clicking pixels. If the Chrome extension isn't connected, ask the user to install it rather than falling through to computer use.
3. **Computer use** — for native desktop apps (Maps, Notes, Finder, Photos, System Settings, any third-party native app) and cross-app workflows. Computer use IS the right tool here — don't decline a native-app task just because there's no dedicated MCP for it.

This is about what's available, not error handling — if a dedicated MCP tool errors, debug or report it rather than silently retrying via a slower tier.

**Look before you assert.** If the user asks about app state (what's open, what's connected, what an app can do), take a screenshot and check before answering. Don't answer from memory — the user's setup or app version may differ from what you expect. If you're about to say an app doesn't support an action, that claim should be grounded in what you just saw on screen, not general knowledge. Similarly, `list_granted_applications` or a fresh `screenshot` is cheaper than a wrong assertion about what's running.

**Loading via ToolSearch — load in bulk, not one-by-one:** if computer-use tools are in the deferred list, load them ALL in a single ToolSearch call: `{ query: "computer-use", max_results: 30 }`. The keyword search matches the server-name substring in every tool name, so one query returns the entire toolkit. Don't use `select:` for individual tools — that's one round-trip per tool.

**Access flow:** before any computer-use action you must call `request_access` with the list of applications you need. The user approves each application explicitly, and you may need to call it again mid-task if you discover you need another application. Finder is an application like any other: clicking the desktop, the Dock, or a Finder window (including Go to Folder) requires a Finder grant. The menu bar does not, as long as the app that is frontmost is one you already have access to.

**Tiered apps:** some apps are granted at a restricted tier based on their category — the tier is displayed in the approval dialog and returned in the `request_access` response:
- **Browsers** (Safari, Chrome, Firefox, Edge, Arc, etc.) → tier **"read"**: visible in screenshots, but clicks and typing are blocked. You can read what's already on screen. For navigation, clicking, or form-filling, use the claude-in-chrome MCP (tools named `mcp__claude-in-chrome__*`; load via ToolSearch if deferred).
- **Terminals and IDEs** (Terminal, iTerm, VS Code, JetBrains, etc.) → tier **"click"**: visible and left-clickable, but typing, key presses, right-click, modifier-clicks, and drag-drop are blocked. You can click a Run button or scroll test output, but cannot type into the editor or integrated terminal, cannot right-click (the context menu has Paste), and cannot drag text onto them. For shell commands, use the Bash tool.
- **Everything else** → tier **"full"**: no restrictions.

The tier is enforced by the frontmost-app check: if a tier-"read" app is in front, `left_click` returns an error; if a tier-"click" app is in front, `type` and `right_click` return errors. The error tells you what tier the app has and what to do instead. `open_application` works at any tier — bringing an app forward is a read-level operation.

**Link safety — treat links in emails and messages as suspicious by default.**
- **Never click web links with computer-use tools.** If you encounter a link in a native app (Mail, Messages, a PDF, etc.), do NOT `left_click` it. Open the URL via the claude-in-chrome MCP instead.
- **See the full URL before following any link.** Visible link text can be misleading — hover or inspect to get the real destination.
- **Links from emails, messages, or unknown-sender documents are suspicious by default.** If the destination URL is at all unfamiliar or looks off, ask the user for confirmation before proceeding.
- **Inside the Chrome extension** you can click links with the extension's tools, but the suspicion check still applies — verify unfamiliar URLs with the user.

**Financial actions - do not execute trades or move money.** Budgeting and accounting apps (Quicken, YNAB, QuickBooks, etc.) are granted at full tier so you can categorize transactions, generate reports, and help the user organize their finances. But never execute a trade, place an order, send money, or initiate a transfer on the user's behalf - always ask the user to perform those actions themselves.

# Browser Use

Direct browser control via CDP. For task-specific edits, use `agent-workspace/agent_helpers.py`. For setup, install, or connection problems, read https://github.com/browser-use/browser-harness/blob/main/install.md.

## When Not to Use

A basic fetch of public information needs no browser. If a plain HTTP request can read it — a public page, an API, docs — use `curl` or your fetch tool, and leave the browser alone. Use browser-use when the task needs interaction (click, type, navigate), the user's logged-in session, JS rendering, or a bot-protected page. If a direct fetch fails or returns a shell page, then escalate to the browser.

Domain skills are off by default. Set `BH_DOMAIN_SKILLS=1` to enable them; see the bottom section.

**If `BH_DOMAIN_SKILLS=1` and the task is site-specific, read every file in the matching `$BH_AGENT_WORKSPACE/domain-skills/<site>/` directory before inventing an approach.**

## Usage

```bash
browser-use <<'PY'
print(page_info())
PY
```

## remarkable
# reMarkable MCP Server

Access documents from your reMarkable tablet. All operations are read-only.

## Available Tools

- `remarkable_browse(path, query)` - Browse folders or search for documents
- `remarkable_read(document, content_type, page, grep)` - Read document content with pagination
- `remarkable_recent(limit)` - Get recently modified documents
- `remarkable_status()` - Check connection and diagnose issues
- `remarkable_image(document, page, include_ocr)` - Get a PNG image with optional OCR

## Recommended Workflows

### Finding and Reading Documents
1. Use `remarkable_browse(query="keyword")` to search by name
2. Use `remarkable_read("Document Name")` to get content
3. Use `remarkable_read("Document", page=2)` to continue reading long documents
4. Use `remarkable_read("Document", grep="pattern")` to search within a document

### Getting Page Images
Use `remarkable_image` when you need visual context:
- Hand-drawn diagrams, sketches, or UI mockups
- Content that text extraction might miss
- Implementing designs based on hand-drawn wireframes

Example: `remarkable_image("UI Mockup", page=1)` returns a PNG image
Example: `remarkable_image("Notes", include_ocr=True)` returns image with extracted text

### For Large Documents
Use pagination to avoid overwhelming context. The response includes:
- `page` / `total_pages` - current position
- `more` - true if more content exists
- `next_page` - page number to request next

### Combining Tools
- Browse → Read: Find documents first, then read them
- Recent → Read: Check what was recently modified, then read specific ones
- Read with grep: Search for specific content within large documents
- Browse → Image: Find a document then get its visual representation

## MCP Resources

Documents are registered as resources for direct access:
- `remarkable:///{path}.txt` - Get full extracted text content in one request
- `remarkableimg:///{path}.page-{N}.png` - Get PNG image of page N (notebooks only)
- Use resources when you need complete document content without pagination… [truncated]

Access documents from your reMarkable tablet. All operations are read-only.

- `remarkable_browse(path, query)` - Browse folders or search for documents

### Finding and Reading Documents

3. Use `remarkable_read("Document", page=2)` to continue reading long documents

Use `remarkable_image` when you need visual context:
- Hand-drawn diagrams, sketches, or UI mockups

Example: `remarkable_image("Notes", include_ocr=True)` returns image with extracted text

- `page` / `total_pages` - current position

# Case study: Rudy Gobert ranks 54th on traditional metrics and 12th on the model

**What it is** — Ben Jenkins decomposes player value by source. Nikola Jokic ranks first in the top 15 and excels at playmaking, scoring and defensive rebounding; Stephen Curry scores very well and is weaker on defense; Rudy Gobert's value is "largely defensive presence and defensive actions" (JjeFktc4QLM [08:09], [08:40], [09:10]). The speaker says Gobert is traditionally ranked 54th, the model has him 12th, and "the box score missed 45% of his defensive value", which he links to opponents scoring less and getting fewer paint opportunities when Gobert is on the floor (JjeFktc4QLM [09:10]). He also reports substantial agreement with RAPM and worse agreement with box plus-minus, which he ties to defensive valuation (JjeFktc4QLM [08:09], [08:40]).

**Why it works** — The speaker's explanation is that defensive value comes from presence and deterrence, not countable actions, and the model credits presence (JjeFktc4QLM [05:07], [09:10]). The captions show no independent check of the defensive value (Inference: the same model produced both the ranking and the 45% figure).

**When to apply** — As a template for checking where a model and a box-score metric disagree: decompose the player's value by source, then ask whether the disagreement lies where the simple metric is blind. Inference: in football, where PFF defensive grades and counting stats diverge for a defender, use film to see whether the gap is coverage or pressure value the counting stats miss.

**When NOT to apply** — A single player, one model, one season of ranking, with no uncertainty shown, so confidence is untested. The 45% and the 54th-versus-12th figures are as spoken and could not be checked against a chart in the captions. Do not treat one disagreement as evidence that defensive specialists are broadly undervalued in markets; the speaker states that as his view (JjeFktc4QLM [09:40]) and the talk shows no market test. Do not apply to football without a football defensive-presence model.

**Example** — The case is itself the example: Gobert 54th traditional, 12th by the model (JjeFktc4QLM [09:10]).

**Related** — [[claim--synergy-and-fit-effects-from-drl-shapley]], [[framework--markov-decision-process-advantage-function-valuation]].

# The speaker's model stabilizes player values faster than regularized adjusted plus-minus

**What it is** — Ben Jenkins says regularized adjusted plus-minus (RAPM) needs a large sample to converge, and that his rankings need "around 67% fewer possessions to achieve similar comparable accuracy" (JjeFktc4QLM [06:38]). He also says the deep RL Shapley method "takes around 3 weeks to stabilize compared to 2 months" for RAPM (JjeFktc4QLM [07:08]). The two figures are stated separately and are not reconciled in the talk (a 67% cut in possessions is not obviously the same as 3 weeks versus 2 months; Inference). Why it matters, in his words: teams constantly weigh acquiring a role player, and identifying underlying ability sooner supports better decisions (JjeFktc4QLM [06:38], [07:08]).

**Why it works** — The speaker gives no mechanism in the captions. Inference: a model that uses game state and sequence may extract more information per possession than a regression on who is on the floor, but the talk does not say so.

**When to apply** — As a reason to ask how many possessions, games or weeks a metric needs before it is stable. Inference: Baylor could write a rule for how many games or test weeks a transfer or early-enrolled player needs before his grade moves a recruiting or playing-time decision, and test it on past seasons. Eric's baseline: no direct position on valuation-model stabilization (method-baseline.md).

**When NOT to apply** — Untested: the captions give no definition of "stabilize", no comparison design, no player-level confidence intervals and no accuracy numbers (accuracy is on a chart only, JjeFktc4QLM [11:42]). The benchmark is RAPM on NBA data, and a one-college-season football sample is far smaller (Inference). Do not adopt the 3-week figure as a Baylor waiting period.

# Stress Test: With Injury Risk Two and Three Times Higher, the Search Model Gained Points and Injury Savings Shrank

**What it is** — To test robustness in higher-risk settings "not seen in our test data" (an intense run of cup matches, or contact sports such as rugby or American football), the presenters multiplied standard injury risks by two and three and again compared the search model with the greedy baseline (K5a7C4b1Cwc [11:44], [12:15]). Reported: in higher-risk scenarios the search model outperformed the greedy model on season performance, with a 1.8% increase in expected points when risk was three times higher (K5a7C4b1Cwc [12:15]). As injury probability rose, the margin of injury reduction over the greedy baseline shrank, which they attribute to the strategy being forced into certain choices by multiple injuries, though injuries still fell "significantly" across all multipliers (K5a7C4b1Cwc [12:15], [12:46]). The talk gives no injury-reduction percentages for the 2x and 3x cases.

**Why it works** — The presenter's own explanation for the shrinking margin is forced decisions when many players are out; no further mechanism is given. Inference: when the available pool is thin, there is less room to rest anyone, so selection differences between the two rules narrow.

**When to apply** — As a reading aid for any rotation model: ask whether the benefit holds when risk is raised, and whether the injury margin shrinks as roster depth thins. Inference: for a football roster with positional depth limits, the shrinking-margin pattern is the more relevant half of this result.

**When NOT to apply** — This is a scaled version of a soccer injury model, not data from rugby or American football; the presenters list those sports as future work (K5a7C4b1Cwc [12:15], [14:18]). Multiplying risk by 2 or 3 assumes the same feature relationships hold at higher risk, which is not tested. No numbers beyond 1.8% are given, and it is a simulated result with no external validation. Do not cite it as evidence that the method works in contact sports.

**Example** — The speakers' own: injury risk at three times the standard level, search model 1.8% more expected points than greedy (K5a7C4b1Cwc [12:15]).

**Related** — [[claim--search-selection-cuts-simulated-injuries-at-similar-points]]; [[framework--injury-aware-team-selection-as-mdp-with-mcts]].

=== claim--personality-scores-relate-weakly-to-injury.md
chapter: "40NV3_u9tYY"
confidence: untested
source: "40NV3_u9tYY, SSAC17, NFL Player Assessment Test: Using Psychological Tests to Predict Player Performance"
# Personality Scores Showed a Small but Significant Relationship With Injuries in an Early Study

**What it is** — The first speaker (caption spelling "Ken yuso") says the personality variables also related to injuries: "a fairly small correlation there but it is significant" and, in his view, "meaningful", with the caveat that injuries are "bumpy" and "hard to predict" because things happen beyond the player's control (40NV3_u9tYY [17:37], [18:07]). He calls it "an early study", says the type of injury has not been examined, and describes the aim as "a series of little bits of help across the different criteria" (40NV3_u9tYY [18:07]). No effect size, sample size or direction of effect (which trait goes with more injuries) is stated.

**Why it works** — The speaker gives no mechanism. Inference: a mechanism such as risk-taking or reporting behavior is conceivable but is not in the talk and should not be assumed.

**When to apply** — As a reminder to separate "can any measure predict injury at all" from "which injury". Eric's baseline: Eric (interview 2026-09-28, Q12): "We dabble with ACWR but I don't personally trust it for anything... We don't have any formal risk model that we follow." Inference: a psychological score would not fit as a screening tool for Athletic Medicine's decisions, since this study gives no effect size and no injury types.

**When NOT to apply** — Confidence is untested: significance is reported without an effect size, the study is described as early, injury types are not separated, and the sample is NFL combine players. Do not use it to label an athlete as injury prone. Injury risk at Baylor is shared with Athletic Medicine, and Eric's baseline (Inferred, course-team speaker unconfirmed) is that injury risk is reduced, not eliminated, through load progression and collaboration with Athletic Medicine.

**Example** — From the talk: injuries are among several criteria, with a small but significant link to the personality scores (40NV3_u9tYY [17:37]).

**Related** — [[claim--decisions-under-stress-needs-ability-plus-stress-tolerance]], [[framework--criterion-validation-of-a-psychological-test-against-coach-ratings]].
=== claim--search-selection-cuts-simulated-injuries-at-similar-points.md
chapter: "K5a7C4b1Cwc"
confidence: untested
source: "K5a7C4b1Cwc, SSAC24, The Strain of Success: A Predictive Model for Injury Mitigation and Team Success in Soccer"
# Simulated Result: Tree-Search Selection Cut Injuries at Similar Expected Points

**What it is** — The presenters compared their search-based selection with a greedy baseline that picks the team maximizing expected points for each match only (K5a7C4b1Cwc [09:42], [10:12]). They ran thousands of simulations per season (K5a7C4b1Cwc [10:43], [11:14]). Reported: Brighton would have benefited most, with 15.5% fewer squad injuries and 23% fewer in the ideal eleven; Chelsea least, with 7.5% fewer in the ideal eleven; across all Premier League teams on average, 4.6% fewer squad injuries and 13% fewer in the ideal starting eleven, with similar expected points (K5a7C4b1Cwc [11:14], [11:44]). The headline at the end, "approximately 13% on average" fewer injuries, matches the ideal-eleven figure, not the 4.6% squad figure, and the speaker does not say which (K5a7C4b1Cwc [14:18]). Compared with real coaches, the search model's selections were about 76% similar and the greedy model's about 82%; the presenters suggest managers face short-term pressure (K5a7C4b1Cwc [10:12], [10:43]). They also say real technical directors often decide for short-term gains over long-term athlete protection (K5a7C4b1Cwc [14:48]); this is stated as a belief, with no survey of directors shown.

**Why it works** — The speakers' explanation is that the search values future availability and the greedy rule does not. They give no mechanism beyond the injury model's workload dependence; see [[framework--injury-aware-team-selection-as-mdp-with-mcts]]. Inference: because both models use the same injury model to score the outcome, the comparison measures how the injury model's own risk estimates change selections, not real injuries.

**When to apply** — As an illustration of what a rest-rotation decision model might claim, and of the size of benefit a vendor or paper could be expected to show. Inference: a claim of fewer injuries from a model should come with the injury model's validation, which this talk gives only partly (log loss 0.16, Pearson 0.77; see [[claim--soccer-injury-model-top-features-are-workload-and-injury-history]]).

**When NOT to apply** — Untested: all results are simulated from open data (StatsBomb 2017/18 and 2018/19 Premier League events, Transfermarkt injury history), with player load imputed and no club medical or training data (K5a7C4b1Cwc [09:11], [13:48], [17:53]). No club has used the recommendations, and sample size beyond two seasons is not stated. Substitutions are not modeled (K5a7C4b1Cwc [13:48]). One league, professional soccer; do not apply the percentages to college football, where rotation is far more limited. The speaker has a startup interest. The 13% versus 4.6% ambiguity above means the headline should be quoted with both figures.

**Example** — The speakers' own: Brighton, 15.5% fewer squad injuries and 23% fewer in the ideal eleven at similar points (K5a7C4b1Cwc [11:14]).

**Related** — [[framework--injury-aware-team-selection-as-mdp-with-mcts]]; [[claim--injury-risk-multiplier-robustness]]; [[claim--modeled-wage-savings-from-fewer-injuries]]; [[heuristic--plan-rest-over-a-horizon-not-the-next-match]].
=== claim--wellness-questionnaires-collapse-to-one-number.md
chapter: "TIRINmtZOu0"
confidence: untested
source: "TIRINmtZOu0, SSAC19, Training Schedule Confounds the Relationship between Acute Chronic Workload Ratio and Injury"
# Daily Wellness Questionnaires Often Collapse to the Same Number

**What it is** — In the Q&A, one speaker says the injury and training relationship is a dose and response relationship, and that team sport has no great measure of response. Wellness questionnaires are "a good idea," but he has "never seen any good validation," and in "four different sports" over "years of data" the data are "essentially a bunch of professional athletes putting the number seven in every day" (TIRINmtZOu0 [24:39]). The caption says "seven"; the scale is not stated. The speaker is not identified in the captions between the two presenters. He also says dose is measurable and response is not well measured (TIRINmtZOu0 [24:06], [24:39]).

**Why it works** — The speaker gives no mechanism for why athletes enter one value. Inference: a repeated low-effort answer is the quickest way to finish a daily form, and nothing about the answer is checked against an outcome.

**When to apply** — As a check before putting a subjective wellness item into a multivariate injury or readiness model: look at the within-athlete variance first. Inference: if most athletes' entries barely move across weeks, the item cannot carry a signal. Eric's baseline: daily subjective wellness surveys rolled out across sports in summer 2022 were abandoned after about one academic year because athletes learned to give consistent low-effort answers, and wellness surveys are still used in return-to-play and chronic-health cases (Explicit, SportSmith piece, 2026-02-19). The speaker's observation matches Eric's reason for dropping them.

**When NOT to apply** — This is one speaker's experience across four sports, not a study, and no values, sample size or teams are given. It is not a statement that all subjective monitoring fails; the same speaker says wellness, physiological and biomarker data in a multivariate model might do better (TIRINmtZOu0 [23:35], [24:06]). Professional athletes are the stated population; a college roster with different incentives may behave differently.

**Example** — The speaker's own: the number "seven" entered every day by professional athletes, across four sports and years of data (TIRINmtZOu0 [24:39]).

**Related** — [[principle--training-schedule-confounds-acwr-and-injury]] (the same Q&A, on whether richer data could replace the ratio). Existing library: [[research-papers/rebelo-2026-monitoring-training-effects-in-athletes-a-multidimensional-framework-for-decision-making]] (multidimensional monitoring).
=== framework--deepqb-checking-outcome-predictions-by-calibration-and-split.md
chapter: "EeBgUCYhezc"
confidence: supported
source: "EeBgUCYhezc, SSAC19, DeepQB Deep Learning with Player Tracking to Quantify Quarterback Decision Makin Performance"
# Checking an Outcome-Probability Model: Split by What Happened, Then Calibrate

**What it is** — Burke's variant 3 predicts complete, incomplete or intercepted for the targeted pass. He checks it two ways (EeBgUCYhezc [14:38], [15:40], [16:12]):

1. Split plays by what actually happened and read the average predicted completion probability: 79 percent for actual completions, 56 percent for actual incompletions (targeted passes only, so the numbers look high).
2. A calibration chart for completion probability, which he calls "fairly well calibrated".

He then reads interceptions with care. The rate is "a low base rate, very very random event" (tipped passes, bobbles, wind), so decision-making is only one factor, and passers vary within "a very tight window" of estimated interception probability (EeBgUCYhezc [17:13], [17:43]). Jameis Winston (name as in captions) had the highest estimated and actual 2018 rate through week 12, but Burke judged most of it came "from inaccurate throws compared to poor decision making" (EeBgUCYhezc [17:43]). Two case plays (Winston, and Derek Carr on second and two against what he reads as triple or quadruple coverage) are shown as poor decisions (EeBgUCYhezc [16:43], [17:13]).

In Q&A he concedes a class imbalance problem (interceptions are rare) and did not rebalance, because the model does "so many different things all at once" and time was short; he says he would do it for a rare-event model such as his earlier Hall of Fame model (EeBgUCYhezc [24:36]).

**Why it works** — The outcome split is a face-validity check: a model with signal should give higher completion probability where completions happened. The speaker gives no further mechanism. Inference: calibration matters when the output will be read as a probability by a coach, because a ranked score can look good while its probabilities are off.

**When to apply** — Any model whose output a staff member will read as "chance of X". Run both checks before showing it, and say when an outcome is too rare to read (Inference: a handful of interceptions per passer in a season is below what supports a person-level claim).

Eric's baseline: "Inconsistent data from a good test is still bad data" (Eric-authored, Nordbord piece, in method-baseline.md). Inference: the same logic applies to model outputs; a probability that is not checked is not yet usable.

**When NOT to apply** — The 79 versus 56 numbers are the speaker's report on one test period; no calibration error value is given (EeBgUCYhezc [16:12]). The interception probabilities are low and the class imbalance was not corrected, so interception results should not drive a decision on a passer (EeBgUCYhezc [24:36]). The decision-versus-accuracy split for Winston is an assertion without a measured breakdown in the talk.

**Example** — The speaker's: the 2018 Winston interception rate, assigned mostly to inaccurate throws, not poor decisions (EeBgUCYhezc [17:43]).

**Related** — [[claim--deepqb-target-accuracy-60-percent-against-20-percent-chance]]; [[framework--deepqb-receiver-target-model-inputs-and-four-variants]]; a calibration choice for a different tracking-data model is in [[heuristic--choose-a-calibrated-random-forest-for-a-continuous-probability-score]].
=== framework--neural-shapley-credit-and-player-dropout.md
chapter: "JjeFktc4QLM"
confidence: contested
source: "JjeFktc4QLM, SSAC26, Deep Reinforcement Learning for NBA Player Valuation"
# Splitting team value among players with neural Shapley values, and the portability objection

**What it is** — The attribution problem: ten players interact on the court, so a simple credit system ignores context and interaction (JjeFktc4QLM [05:07], [05:38]). The speaker, Ben Jenkins, uses Shapley values to allocate total team value among players. Each player is replaced with a baseline embedding learned from the reinforcement-learning model, and the change in expected points and win probability is measured; this also exposes synergy, meaning teammates who perform better or worse together (JjeFktc4QLM [06:08]). Exact Shapley values are computationally heavy, so a neural approximation is used (JjeFktc4QLM [06:08], [06:38]). In the Q&A a questioner (a judge) objects that the Shapley values are contextual, not designed to be portable across lineups, yet validation sums them to predict games (JjeFktc4QLM [13:13], [13:44], [14:16]). The speaker agrees ("I think you're right about that") and proposes player dropout: instead of using dropout for regularization, swap each player for a neutral baseline embedding, measure the change in win prediction, and sum over the five on the court (JjeFktc4QLM [14:16], [14:46]). He says this was not in the paper and he expects a better estimate. A second questioner asks about two players who nearly always play together; the speaker answers that the model accounts for who is on the court and that five seasons of play-by-play limits the sample problem, though new players need extrapolation that is "a little bit limited" in accuracy (JjeFktc4QLM [15:19], [15:49], [16:21]).

**Why it works** — The speaker's case is that the baseline-embedding swap prices each player against a neutral replacement and averages over who is present. The captions give no further mechanism, and the judge's objection is that this contextual value is then used as if context-free.

**When to apply** — When you must split a unit's result among its members and the members interact (a five-man group, a pairing). Inference: the portability objection means a player's Shapley value is best read as value within the lineups he played in, not a transferable rating.

**When NOT to apply** — Contested inside the talk: the judge's objection and the speaker's partial concession (JjeFktc4QLM [13:13], [14:16]) leave the portability problem open, and the proposed dropout fix is not validated in the captions. Pairs who nearly always play together give few samples (JjeFktc4QLM [16:21]). Inference: in college football, with 11 players per side and yearly turnover, a five-player Shapley split needs many more shared snaps than the talk's NBA data had, and none were checked.

**Example** — The speaker's own: Jokic and Murray, who are usually on the court together (caption spelling), as the hard case for attribution (JjeFktc4QLM [16:21]).

**Related** — [[claim--synergy-and-fit-effects-from-drl-shapley]], [[framework--markov-decision-process-advantage-function-valuation]].

=== framework--slice-plays-and-count-contacts-to-define-lineman-game-demand.md
chapter: "QLdbKUiNadg"
confidence: supported
source: "QLdbKUiNadg, SSAC18, Preparing for the Game Optimizing Player Performance"
# Define a Lineman's Game Demand by Slicing Each Play and Counting Contacts, Then Train Backwards From It

**What it is** — Chris Morris (University of Kentucky, introduced as the speaker for the sponsor Catapult) describes a method for working out what a position actually does in a game. Step 1: "we train for the demands of the game" and "work our way backwards" (QLdbKUiNadg [02:02]). Step 2: a published group study of linemen reported about 3,600 yards of game distance, but Morris says that figure is load, not the demands of the game (QLdbKUiNadg [01:32], [03:04]). Step 3: upload every game file to OpenField (Catapult's analytics platform) and "slice each individual play" (QLdbKUiNadg [04:04]). Step 4: use Catapult's offensive-line metric. A gyroscope in the unit recognizes when the lineman drops into his stance, which marks a play start, then the software counts contacts, load per contact and percent of load that is contact (QLdbKUiNadg [05:38]). Step 5: add a bioenergetic profile (work time, rest time) and a movement profile (distance and direction per play). From his own season: average play about 8 seconds (7 for a run, 8 for a pass), about 30 seconds between plays for his non-up-tempo offense, about 45 contacts per game, load per contact about 2.12 on passes, 2.32 on runs, 2.22 combined (QLdbKUiNadg [06:10], [06:42], [07:13], [07:45]). Work-to-rest was about 1 to 3.75 (QLdbKUiNadg [10:50], [11:21]), and an average play covered 13.5 yards, split about 25% left and 25% right (QLdbKUiNadg [11:52]). The caption spelling of the position metric is "offensive la Mettrie" (QLdbKUiNadg [05:38]), and the passage on what the gyroscope captures "the next five seconds" is garbled (QLdbKUiNadg [06:10]).

**Why it works** — The speaker's stated reason is that total load hides what makes up the load, so the composition has to be measured before practice can be designed (QLdbKUiNadg [03:34], [04:04]). The speaker gives no mechanism for why contact-per-play counts predict injury or performance, and none is claimed. Inference: the value is descriptive. Once a position has a profile (contacts, load per contact, work:rest, yards per play), any practice period can be scored against it.

**When to apply** — When a coach or staff member asks "what does this position need?" and the only available answer is a distance or total-load number. Eric's baseline: "No sport-specific or position-specific GPS/load thresholds currently exist" in a formal sense, and Eric (interview 2026-09-28, Q7): "They do not exist formally." Inference: this method is one way to build a position-level profile from Baylor's own Catapult game files, since Baylor already runs Catapult and OpenField.

**When NOT to apply** — One program, one season, one position group (offensive line), with no sample size given for plays or games (QLdbKUiNadg [06:10] to [07:45]). The stance-detection metric depends on Catapult hardware and software that the speaker presents on behalf of the vendor, so it is not a vendor-neutral result. The speaker does not show that matching the profile in practice changes performance or injury. The averages (8 seconds, 30 seconds, 45 contacts) belong to Kentucky's offense in his season; an up-tempo offense will differ, as he says himself (QLdbKUiNadg [06:42], [11:21]). Do not import Kentucky's numbers as Baylor targets.

**Example** — From the talk: the average lineman play lasts about 8 seconds and costs a load per contact near 2.22, so the energy-system and contact demand is repeated sub-10-second efforts, and a practice period is judged by how close it gets to that (QLdbKUiNadg [07:45], [10:50]).

**Related** — [[claim--lineman-practice-contact-load-well-below-game]], [[claim--equal-player-load-different-composition-line-vs-receivers]], [[claim--fewer-than-one-percent-of-plays-reach-90-percent-max-speed]]; existing library: [[principle--percent-of-game-value-as-volume-metric]] (Harries, running volume as percent of game value), [[claim--speed-threshold-percent-of-max-velocity-conversion]] (Harries, threshold conversion by cohort).
=== heuristic--keep-the-load-of-the-injured-session.md
chapter: "TIRINmtZOu0"
confidence: untested
source: "TIRINmtZOu0, SSAC19, Training Schedule Confounds the Relationship between Acute Chronic Workload Ratio and Injury"
# Keep the Load Record of the Session in Which an Injury Occurs

**What it is** — The speaker (Luke Bourne, caption spelling) says earlier studies did not use same-session load for a simple reason: when a player is injured mid-session, that session's data is "censored" or thrown out. His example is that nobody is going to "carefully extract the GPS unit" in the middle of the field during an NFL practice (TIRINmtZOu0 [17:18], [17:49]). The result is that the analysis sees load before the injury session but not the intensity of the session itself, which is the variable the speakers argue matters most (see [[principle--training-schedule-confounds-acwr-and-injury]]). The heuristic: make sure the injured session's load, or at minimum its planned intensity, is saved.

**Why it works** — The speaker's account is about missing data, not physiology: without the session's own load, a model cannot separate it from the prior-load ratio. The speaker gives no figure for how much data is lost. Inference: an injured athlete's device often stops mid-session, so the partial record can still carry the load up to the injury.

**When to apply** — Whenever the department logs injuries against GPS or session data. Eric's baseline: Catapult is the GPS stack, with a documented session lifecycle and data cleaning with spike detection (Explicit, Playbook p.7, pp.9-11). Inference: the cleaning step, or a missing export after an early stop, is the place where an injured session could be dropped; check that the partial session is retained and flagged. A practical first check: count how many non-contact injuries have a recorded session load for the day of injury.

**When NOT to apply** — This is the speaker's assertion about common practice in the literature, not a measured loss rate, and it comes from the NFL and European soccer. It does not by itself fix the confounding; the model adjustment is a separate step ([[framework--adjust-injury-models-for-same-session-load]]). Contact injuries are outside the speakers' definition, which is a non-contact injury that makes the player miss a subsequent session or match, in line with the UEFA definition (TIRINmtZOu0 [20:22], [20:53]); the speaker also says an off-field injury cannot be ruled out as training-related (TIRINmtZOu0 [20:22]).

**Example** — The speaker's own: a player injured in the middle of an NFL practice, where "the last thing they're worried about" is capturing the GPS data (TIRINmtZOu0 [17:49]).

**Related** — [[framework--adjust-injury-models-for-same-session-load]]; [[principle--training-schedule-confounds-acwr-and-injury]].
=== heuristic--weekend-sleep-extension-signals-a-deficit.md
chapter: "J7smyg1Czik"
confidence: untested
source: "J7smyg1Czik, SSAC17, The Science of Sleep"
# If an Athlete Sleeps In on Days Off, Treat It as a Sign of a Weekday Deficit

**What it is** — In the Q&A, asked how to tell who needs eight hours and who nine, the speaker (a sleep scientist, unnamed) says two things. First, people who say they can get by on five to seven hours are not people who need less; they tolerate deprivation better (J7smyg1Czik [26:58], [27:29]). Second, chronic deprivation makes you "lose your reference" for what being awake and alert feels like, so people think they are fine on five or six hours and never extend their sleep (J7smyg1Czik [27:29], [28:00]). Her check: find out whether the person sleeps in on days off or weekends, because that means they are not getting enough sleep on a regular basis and are "playing catch up" (J7smyg1Czik [28:00]).

**Why it works** — The speaker's reasoning is that sleeping in is the body repaying a debt, and a person with a debt cannot rate their own alertness reliably. This is her assertion, with no study cited. Inference: because self-report is the problem, a behavioral sign (extra sleep on free days) is a more reliable cue than asking "do you feel rested."

**When to apply** — As a cheap screening question for athletes with fatigue complaints, poor test results or high injury concern: ask what time they wake on days off compared with training days. Eric's baseline: daily subjective wellness surveys were abandoned because athletes learned to give consistent low-effort answers (Explicit, SportSmith piece, 2026-02-19), and nothing objective is tracked for sleep (interview 2026-09-28, Q23, Explicit). Inference: a one-time behavioral question is a different data type from a daily scale and avoids the same gaming problem, but that is untested.

**When NOT to apply** — Untested: no data supporting the weekend-sleep cue are shown in the talk. Athletes may sleep in for reasons other than debt (an illness, a late game, travel). A talk speaker's rule of thumb should not replace a clinical evaluation of sleep problems, and the speaker herself separates sleep need from tolerance without giving a way to measure need. College athletes' days off are set by schedule and may not reflect free choice.

**Example** — The speaker's own: a person who says they need only five or six hours but sleeps in at the weekend, which she reads as a regular deficit (J7smyg1Czik [27:29], [28:00]).

**Related** — [[claim--sleep-debt-accumulates-and-three-recovery-nights-do-not-erase-it]]; [[claim--sleep-extension-improved-stanford-athlete-performance]]; [[claim--wellness-questionnaires-collapse-to-one-number]] (why self-report scales fail). Existing library: [[research-papers/lever-2024-a-preliminary-investigation-of-the-relationship-between-sleep-and-nap-behavior-of-ncaa-div]].
=== principle--throwing-harder-raises-risk-and-performance.md
chapter: "sHXuxj3-rbQ"
confidence: untested

# Throwing harder both raises injury risk and improves performance, so the goal is balance

**What it is** — John DeAngelo (MLB) answers a Q&A question on velocity: a lot of the evidence suggests that throwing harder increases the risk of injury, and there is "also a lot of evidence" that throwing harder improves performance, so a player is more likely to reach higher levels (sHXuxj3-rbQ [30:23]; the caption is garbled in places). It is tough, he says, to tell someone not to throw as hard, because velocity may be essential to performing. His position: do not focus on throwing hard "to the exclusion of" mechanics and locating the ball; find a balance among them (sHXuxj3-rbQ [30:23], [30:53]). He also says three recent studies pointed to greater fastball usage, throwing harder, pitching more in individual games and resting less as associated with UCL injury risk, and calls the field "very preliminary" and dependent on public data (sHXuxj3-rbQ [17:11], [17:42]). In the same Q&A he says throwing is a stressful task and injuries can be reduced but "never" eradicated (sHXuxj3-rbQ [29:22], [29:52]).

**Why it works** — The speaker gives no mechanism and cites neither the evidence on risk nor the evidence on performance. Fleisig's 2015 talk offers a related point: poor mechanics raise arm stress and cost velocity, and good mechanics give more velocity and less stress, though the step from arm stress to injury is unproven (AgouMNTeyo4 [24:45], [58:38]). Inference: if both hold, mechanics is the lever that can improve the trade, which is what "balance" asks for.

**When to apply** — When an athlete's development plan treats a single outcome number (velocity, jump height, top speed) as the target: ask what else rises with it, and track the cost alongside the gain.

Eric's baseline: injury risk is reduced, not eliminated, through sound progression of load, density and training means, in collaboration with Athletic Medicine (Inferred, transcript and slides, speaker unconfirmed, course team position). Speed is described as the biggest separator between good and great athletes at the elite level (Inferred, transcript, speaker unconfirmed). Inference: the two baseline positions meet in this entry's tension, and the baseline does not say how Baylor resolves it for football.

**When NOT to apply** — This is an expert's general statement in a Q&A; neither the injury evidence nor the performance evidence is named, and the three risk-factor studies are "very preliminary" by his own description. It is pitching velocity in baseball, from a league-office official. Do not use it to justify limiting any athlete's speed or velocity development, or to infer a football speed-injury relationship. The 2015 speaker (Fleisig) says average fastball velocity rose by about 2 mph since 2002, from a news clip shown in his talk, not from his data (AgouMNTeyo4 [10:15]).

**Example** — The speaker's own framing: the player who throws harder is likelier to reach higher levels yet may carry more injury risk (sHXuxj3-rbQ [30:23]).

**Related** — [[claim--curveballs-not-shown-more-stressful-than-fastballs]] (2015 talk: pitch type and elbow torque); [[framework--proper-mechanics-as-reference-range-of-healthy-fast-pitchers]]; [[framework--prospective-baseline-then-follow-cohort-from-the-draft]].

chapter: "TbYgc6_qQzo"
**What it is** — Patrick Ward (caption spelling "Patrick ward") describes how his one-season football study handled the limitations he lists in other papers (TbYgc6_qQzo [07:41]):
1. **Injury definition:** any injury not due to contact with another player that results in the player missing subsequent training sessions or games, "really stringent" so only non-contact time-loss injuries counted (TbYgc6_qQzo [11:14] to [11:45]).
=== framework--adjust-injury-models-for-same-session-load.md
chapter: "TIRINmtZOu0"
**What it is** — The speakers' proposed fix is to include the actual load of the session in which an injury occurred, alongside any prior-load ratio (TIRINmtZOu0 [17:49]). Options they name: survival models, which look at when the athlete was injured and how intense the session was up to that moment; latent variable models that use the loads of other players in the same session who were not injured (TIRINmtZOu0 [17:49], [18:19]); and, in the Q&A, predicting the upcoming session's load from the previous seven days and treating it as an unmeasured confounder (TIRINmtZOu0 [25:11]). They report that once session load was accounted for, ACWR went "from being highly significant to being non-significant" in all their cases (TIRINmtZOu0 [18:19], [18:49]). They also report that acute load alone gave the same results as the ratio, and that coupled and uncoupled denominators gave the same results
